precepts.text: The Lord warned he would bring evil from the north, a great destruction, which is the army of Babylon that came against Judah.
precepts.point: This came upon Judah at the commandment of the Lord to remove them out of his sight for the sins of Manasseh and the innocent blood he shed, which the Lord would not pardon.

note.label: 2 Kings 24: Judah Carried Away for the Sins of Manasseh

precepts.why:
Jeremiah was told, “Set up the standard toward Zion: retire, stay not: for I will bring evil from the north, and a great destruction.” That evil from the north is the army of Babylon, the very bands the Lord sent against Judah.

In the days of Jehoiakim, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came up, and Jehoiakim served him three years and then turned and rebelled. So the Lord sent “bands of the Chaldees, and bands of the Syrians, and bands of the Moabites, and bands of the children of Ammon” against Judah “to destroy it, according to the word of the Lord, which he spake by his servants the prophets.” The warning from the north was that word, now fulfilled.

It did not come by chance: “Surely at the commandment of the Lord came this upon Judah, to remove them out of his sight, for the sins of Manasseh”, and for the innocent blood he shed, “which the Lord would not pardon.” The Lord warned of a great destruction, and then he brought it.

precepts.text: Isaiah prophesied to Hezekiah that all in his house and the treasures his fathers had laid up would be carried to Babylon, fulfilled in this robbing of the temple.
precepts.point: He carried Jehoiachin, the king's mother, wives, and officers to Babylon, along with the men of might and craftsmen and smiths, wanting them to build for him what they had built in their own land, as conquering nations always used Israel's skill and industry.

note.label: 2 Kings 24: Judah Carried Away for the Sins of Manasseh

precepts.why:
Isaiah told Hezekiah, “Behold, the days come, that all that is in thine house, and that which thy fathers have laid up in store until this day, shall be carried to Babylon: nothing shall be left, saith the Lord.”

Here it is fulfilled. Nebuchadnezzar “carried out thence all the treasures of the house of the Lord, and the treasures of the king’s house, and cut in pieces all the vessels of gold which Solomon king of Israel had made in the temple of the Lord, as the Lord had said.” The robbing of the temple is exactly what Isaiah prophesied: nothing left.

And not only the treasures. He carried away all Jerusalem, the princes, the mighty men of valour, ten thousand captives, “and all the craftsmen and smiths: none remained, save the poorest sort of the people of the land.” Jehoiachin, the king’s mother, his wives and his officers went to Babylon too. Babylon wanted the craftsmen and smiths to build for it what they had built in their own land, for conquering nations have always used Israel’s skill and industry.

precepts.text: Jeremiah, shut up in prison, warned Zedekiah he would not escape but be delivered to Babylon, see the king face to face, and not prosper in fighting the Chaldeans.
precepts.point: Through the anger of the Lord it came to pass in Jerusalem and Judah, until he had cast them out of his presence, that Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

note.label: 2 Kings 24: Judah Carried Away for the Sins of Manasseh

precepts.why:
In “the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah”, when “the king of Babylon’s army besieged Jerusalem”, Jeremiah was “shut up in the court of the prison”. Zedekiah had shut him up for prophesying that the Lord would give the city into the hand of the king of Babylon.

Jeremiah warned him plainly: “Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him mouth to mouth, and his eyes shall behold his eyes”. He would be led to Babylon, “and there shall he be until I visit him, saith the Lord: though ye fight with the Chaldeans, ye shall not prosper.”

That is the Zedekiah of this passage. The king of Babylon made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin’s father’s brother, king in his stead and changed his name to Zedekiah. He reigned eleven years and “did that which was evil in the sight of the Lord, according to all that Jehoiakim had done.” And “through the anger of the Lord” it came to pass that Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon, until the Lord had cast Judah out from his presence. He was warned, he rebelled anyway, and he could not prosper against the Chaldeans.

precepts.text: Nebuchadnezzar carried the real king Jehoiachin to Babylon and made his father's brother Mattaniah king in his stead, changing his name to Zedekiah, a puppet king set up by the oppressor.
precepts.point: Zedekiah was not of the royal lineage per se, and Zedekiah was not really his name; to see how he became king we go back to when Babylon took the real king away.

note.label: Jeremiah 52: The Fall of Jerusalem and the Puppet King Zedekiah

precepts.why:
To see how Zedekiah became king, go back to when Babylon took the real king away. Nebuchadnezzar “carried away Jehoiachin to Babylon, and the king’s mother, and the king’s wives, and his officers, and the mighty of the land”, with “all the men of might, even seven thousand, and craftsmen and smiths a thousand, all that were strong and apt for war”.

Then “the king of Babylon made Mattaniah his father’s brother king in his stead, and changed his name to Zedekiah.” So Zedekiah was not of the royal lineage per se, and Zedekiah was not really his name. He was Mattaniah, the real king's father's brother, a puppet king set up by the oppressor. That is the Zedekiah who “was one and twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.”

precepts.text: Nebuchadnezzar carried away all Jerusalem, the princes and mighty men of valour, craftsmen and smiths, leaving only the poorest sort, and made Mattaniah king, changing his name to Zedekiah.
precepts.point: When our people do well financially, get a good education, and buy into the pick-yourself-up-by-the-bootstraps idea that everyone has the same opportunity, the smart ones are removed from the ghetto so they will not be there to cause the uprising.

note.label: Ezekiel 17: The Riddle of the Two Eagles

precepts.why:
This is the history behind “the king of Babylon is come to Jerusalem, and hath taken the king thereof, and the princes thereof”. Nebuchadnezzar “carried away all Jerusalem, and all the princes, and all the mighty men of valour, even ten thousand captives, and all the craftsmen and smiths: none remained, save the poorest sort of the people of the land.”

He carried Jehoiachin to Babylon, with the king's mother, the king's wives, his officers and “the mighty of the land”: seven thousand men of might, a thousand craftsmen and smiths, “all that were strong and apt for war”. Then he “made Mattaniah his father’s brother king in his stead, and changed his name to Zedekiah.” That is the king's seed he made a covenant with and took an oath of.

The mighty, the skilled, the strong: everyone who could have lifted the kingdom up was taken, and only the poorest sort were left. That is what it means for the kingdom to be base, so that it might not lift itself up, but stand only by keeping his covenant.

And what did they have in Babylon? Idols. What did they have in Assyria? Idols.

And over time, what did we do? We lost our identity, and we lost our connection to God's laws, and we started worshipping idols. So we were Gentiles carried away to these dumb idols. It is talking about Israel.
